schema_note: domain in {diagnosis, differential, treatment, resistance, comorbidity, monitoring, prevention, notification, social_support}. divergence_type in {prevalence_dependent, protocol_specific, resource_dependent, epidemiology_specific}. still_diverges_as_of is the YYYY-MM this row was last confirmed against the cited primary sources.

rows.decision_point: Which test is used first for a patient with presumptive pulmonary TB: molecular (NAAT) testing, or sputum smear microscopy plus culture?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP directs providers to use rapid molecular diagnostics (CBNAAT/TrueNat) upfront wherever possible as the initial test for presumptive pulmonary TB. In the standard workflow, one specimen is tested by NAAT and, only if TB is detected, a second specimen proceeds to LPA/liquid culture for the resistance-detection cascade -- culture is not a routine parallel requirement for treatment initiation.

ntep_citation.doc: NTEP Knowledge Base, "Principles of TB Diagnosis under NTEP", Central TB Division
ntep_citation.section: Diagnostic algorithm for presumptive pulmonary TB

rows.western_position: The standing ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline recommends AFB smear microscopy in ALL patients suspected of pulmonary TB (Recommendation 5, strong recommendation) and both liquid and solid mycobacterial culture on every specimen (Recommendation 6, culture is 'the gold standard'), while a diagnostic NAAT on the initial respiratory specimen is only a conditional recommendation based on low-quality evidence (Recommendation 7) -- markedly weaker than WHO's own 2024 strong/high-certainty recommendation for Xpert as the initial test (see notes).

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Official ATS/IDSA/CDC Clinical Practice Guidelines: Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33

rows.notes: WHO's own Module 3 (3rd ed., 20 Mar 2024) now gives a strong, high-certainty recommendation for Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra as the initial diagnostic test 'rather than smear microscopy/culture and phenotypic DST' (data/protocols/WHO_Module3_Diagnosis_2024.pdf, Recommendations 1-5, p.5). So NTEP and WHO now agree; the divergence that persists is between NTEP/WHO and the still-current 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline, which has a materially weaker, conditional recommendation for NAAT and treats smear+culture as mandatory. A vignette should not accept 'my program follows WHO guidance' as equivalent to 'my program follows US clinical practice guidance' on this point.

rows.decision_point: Is rapid molecular rifampicin-resistance testing (DST) performed for every newly diagnosed TB patient, or only for patients meeting specific risk criteria?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP defines 'Universal DST' as universal access to rapid drug-resistance testing for at least rifampicin (and further testing for at least fluoroquinolones once RR is detected) for ALL TB patients, preferably before treatment initiation and within a maximum of 15 days of diagnosis -- not contingent on any individual risk factor.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guidelines for Management of Drug Resistant TB (27-3-2025)

rows.western_position: The 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline recommends rapid molecular DST for rifampin (with or without isoniazid) only for AFB-smear-positive or NAAT-positive patients who ALSO meet at least one of: prior TB treatment; birth in or >=1 year residence in a country with at least moderate TB incidence (>=20/100,000) or high primary MDR-TB prevalence (>=2%); contact of an MDR-TB patient; or HIV infection -- a risk-targeted approach, not a universal one.

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33
western_citation.section: Rapid molecular drug-susceptibility testing recommendation (p. e3)

rows.notes: A vignette in the western_control arm with none of the four US risk criteria should not have rapid RR-DST as an expected action under the cited 2017 framework, whereas the same case in the india_high arm should.

rows.decision_point: How is extrapulmonary TB worked up microbiologically when bacteriological confirmation is difficult?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP offers upfront NAAT (CBNAAT/TrueNat/LPA) on essentially any accessible extrapulmonary specimen type as the first-line microbiological tool, alongside histopathology, ADA/biochemical testing of body fluids, and imaging (CXR/CT/USG/MRI/PET). Where bacteriological confirmation still cannot be achieved despite these efforts, clinical judgment by an experienced clinician, supported by suggestive laboratory tests, may be used to diagnose EPTB.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Training Module on Extrapulmonary TB (24-03-2023)
ntep_citation.section: Diagnosis of EPTB / Tools for Microbiological Confirmation of EPTB (p. 26)

rows.western_position: The 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline's NAAT recommendation (Recommendation 7) is a general, pulmonary-specimen-focused, conditional/low-quality-evidence recommendation; the guideline does not give extrapulmonary specimens the same upfront-NAAT-first framing NTEP uses, and continues to anchor extrapulmonary workup around culture and histology as the reference standard.

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33

rows.notes: Weaker citation than most rows in this table: the 2017 guideline is not extrapulmonary-specific, so the western_position here is inferred from its general NAAT stance rather than a dedicated EPTB recommendation. Treat this row as lower-confidence than DIV-001/002 pending a fetch of an EPTB-specific western guideline.

rows.decision_point: Is mycobacterial culture a mandatory parallel test for every patient with suspected TB, or reserved for the resistance-detection cascade after a positive molecular test?
rows.ntep_position: In NTEP's standard workflow, culture is reached only as the second step of a cascade after an initial NAAT-positive result (for LPA/liquid culture resistance testing) -- it is not a universally mandated parallel test performed on every presumptive-TB patient regardless of the NAAT result.

ntep_citation.doc: NTEP Knowledge Base, "Principles of TB Diagnosis under NTEP", Central TB Division

rows.western_position: The 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline's Recommendation 6 calls for both liquid and solid mycobacterial culture 'for every specimen obtained from an individual with suspected TB disease,' describing culture as the gold-standard microbiologic test regardless of NAAT or smear result.

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33

rows.decision_point: For diagnosing TB infection (TBI/LTBI), is IGRA preferred over TST when the person has a history of BCG vaccination?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP treats TST and IGRA as interchangeable options for TBI testing, to be offered 'wherever available' -- TPT eligibility and initiation are not gated on which test is used, or on using either test at all, for the highest-priority groups (see DIV-010/011).

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment in India (2021)
ntep_citation.section: 3.3.1 Tuberculin Skin Test / 3.3.2 Interferon-Gamma Release Assay (p. 10)

rows.western_position: The 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline's Recommendation 1a explicitly recommends IGRA rather than TST for individuals with a history of BCG vaccination (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence), precisely because BCG vaccination confounds TST interpretation.

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33

rows.decision_point: Is the first-line drug-sensitive TB regimen given daily throughout treatment, or can the continuation phase use intermittent (thrice- or twice-weekly) dosing?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's stated principle (except for confirmed DR-TB) is to administer daily fixed-dose combination first-line ATT in appropriate weight bands under direct observation, for both the intensive phase (2HRZE) and continuation phase (4HRE) -- there is no programmatic intermittent-dosing option for drug-sensitive TB.

ntep_citation.doc: ICMR/Dept. of Health Research (MoHFW), Standard Treatment Workflow: Drug Sensitive-TB Treatment as per NTEP (March 2022)

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline strongly recommends daily intensive-phase dosing (Recommendation 3a), but conditionally permits thrice-weekly (Recommendation 3b) or, when DOT is difficult, twice-weekly (Recommendation 3c) dosing in the continuation phase for patients who are HIV-negative and at low relapse risk (noncavitary and/or smear-negative disease).

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Official ATS/CDC/IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines: Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195

rows.notes: A vignette should not accept an intermittent continuation-phase regimen as 'standard NTEP practice' -- it is a western_control-arm option only, and only for low-relapse-risk, HIV-negative patients even there.

rows.decision_point: Is anti-TB drug dosing determined by a fixed weight-band tablet count, or calculated individually in mg/kg?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP dispenses first-line ATT as fixed-dose-combination tablets in discrete weight-band categories (e.g., 25-34 kg, 35-49 kg, 50-64 kg, 65-75 kg, >75 kg for adults; six paediatric weight bands), with a defined FDC tablet count per band rather than a per-kilogram calculation performed at the point of care.

ntep_citation.doc: ICMR/Dept. of Health Research (MoHFW), Standard Treatment Workflow: Drug Sensitive-TB Treatment as per NTEP (March 2022)
ntep_citation.section: Number of tablets (FDCs) by weight category, adult and paediatric tables

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline's drug dosing table specifies doses in mg/kg ranges (e.g., isoniazid 5 mg/kg daily, rifampin 10 mg/kg daily, with defined mg/kg ranges) calculated per patient rather than assigned via fixed tablet-count bands.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195

rows.decision_point: When bacteriological non-conversion or slow clinical response occurs, is regimen extension governed by a specific evidence-based rule, or by individualized physician discretion?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's standard treatment workflow leaves extension of the continuation phase to the treating physician's case-by-case judgment for disseminated TB or slow response, without a codified rule tied to specific radiographic or bacteriological criteria (distinct fixed extensions apply only to specific extrapulmonary sites such as CNS/skeletal TB).

ntep_citation.doc: ICMR/Dept. of Health Research (MoHFW), Standard Treatment Workflow: Drug Sensitive-TB Treatment as per NTEP (March 2022)
ntep_citation.section: Continuation phase notes: 'In disseminated TB or slow response treating physician may extend on case to case basis'

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline gives a specific expert-opinion rule: patients with cavitation on the initial chest radiograph AND a positive culture at completion of 2 months of therapy should have the continuation phase extended by an additional 3 months (7-month continuation phase, 9 months total), based on relapse rates of ~20% vs 2% for patients with neither risk factor.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195

rows.decision_point: For a household/close contact of a patient with fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR/RR-TB, is a fixed standardized preventive regimen given, or is treatment itself only conditionally recommended with an individualized regimen if given?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's 2024 TPT addendum specifies a fixed, standardized preventive regimen for household contacts of drug-resistant index cases: 6 months of daily levofloxacin (6Lfx) for contacts of fluoroquinolone-susceptible MDR-TB, or 4 months of daily rifampicin (4R) for contacts of isoniazid mono/poly-resistant TB -- offered as a routine part of programmatic TPT.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidance document on 1HP TPT regimen (addendum to the 2021 PMTPT guidelines, Dec 2024)
ntep_citation.section: TPT target group, strategy, and treatment options table (p. 1-2)

rows.western_position: The 2019 ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA guideline only conditionally recommends offering LTBI treatment to MDR-TB contacts at all, versus observation alone ('conditional recommendation, very low certainty in the evidence') -- and if treatment is given, the regimen and duration (6-12 months of a later-generation fluoroquinolone alone or with a second drug) are individualized to the source case's susceptibility pattern rather than fixed.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis: An Official ATS/CDC/ERS/IDSA Clinical Practice Guideline, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2019;200(10):e93-e142

rows.notes: Fetched via WebFetch against the journal page rather than a locally archived PDF (thoracic.org's direct PDF link 404'd/redirected -- see FETCH_LOG.md). A vignette should not treat 'observation only, no preventive treatment' as wrong in the western_control arm the way it would be in the india_high arm.

rows.decision_point: Are all household contacts of a pulmonary TB patient offered TB preventive treatment (TPT) regardless of age, with treatment proceeding even if TBI testing is unavailable?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's 2021 TPT guideline states that ALL household contacts of pulmonary TB patients, regardless of age, should be given TPT after ruling out active TB. Contacts under 5 years receive TPT empirically without TBI testing; contacts 5 years and older and adults should be offered CXR and TBI testing wherever available, but 'TPT must not be deferred' if such testing is unavailable.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment in India (2021)
ntep_citation.section: 2.1.2 All household contacts of pulmonary TB patients (p. 5)

rows.western_position: The CDC/NTCA 2020 guideline is scoped as treatment of confirmed latent TB infection -- its recommended regimens (3HP, 4R, 3HR preferred) are framed as treatment once LTBI has been established, implying a test-confirm-then-treat sequence rather than NTEP's empiric-if-testing-unavailable approach for household contacts.

western_citation.doc: Guidelines for the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection: Recommendations from NTCA and CDC, 2020, MMWR Recomm Rep 2020;69(1):1-11
western_citation.section: Preferred regimens (p. 3); document title and scope

rows.notes: The western_position here is partly inferential (the CDC document's own scope/title implies test-then-treat rather than stating it as an explicit contrast with empiric treatment) -- the dedicated CDC targeted-testing eligibility guideline was not fetched this session (see FETCH_LOG.md). This is the single most important correction from the prior draft: NTEP does NOT limit TPT to child contacts under 6 -- see UNVERIFIED.md and SUMMARY.md.

rows.decision_point: For a person living with HIV, is TB preventive treatment started without requiring a positive TBI (TST/IGRA) test?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's TPT guideline explicitly states that testing for TBI by TST or IGRA is NOT a requirement for initiating TPT in people living with HIV (or in children under 5) -- TPT proceeds empirically once active TB disease has been ruled out.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidelines for Programmatic Management of Tuberculosis Preventive Treatment in India (2021)

rows.western_position: The CDC/NTCA 2020 guideline lists 3 months of once-weekly isoniazid-rifapentine (3HP) as a preferred regimen 'strongly recommended for adults and children aged >=2 years, including HIV-positive persons,' but frames this within a guideline for treatment of confirmed LTBI, without stating an equivalent empiric-without-testing exception for PLHIV.

western_citation.doc: Guidelines for the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection: Recommendations from NTCA and CDC, 2020, MMWR Recomm Rep 2020;69(1):1-11
western_citation.section: Preferred Regimens -- Three Months of Weekly Isoniazid Plus Rifapentine (p. 3)

rows.notes: Same inferential caveat as DIV-010 regarding the CDC document's implicit test-first framing.

rows.decision_point: Is the 1-month daily rifapentine-isoniazid (1HP) regimen a programmatically available TPT option?
rows.ntep_position: As of a December 2024 addendum, NTEP has formally adopted 1HP (28 daily doses of isoniazid + rifapentine) as a TPT option for persons aged >=13 years, including PLHIV, household contacts of drug-sensitive TB, and other expanded risk groups.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidance document on shorter one-month daily isoniazid and rifapentine (1HP) TPT regimen (Dec 2024)

rows.western_position: The CDC/NTCA 2020 guideline -- the standing US regimen guideline -- cites the same underlying 1HP evidence (the BRIEF-TB/A5279 trial) only in its bibliography and does not list 1HP among its recommended/preferred/alternative regimens.

western_citation.doc: Guidelines for the Treatment of Latent Tuberculosis Infection: Recommendations from NTCA and CDC, 2020, MMWR Recomm Rep 2020;69(1):1-11
western_citation.section: References (1HP trial cited as background evidence only, not as a listed regimen)

rows.notes: This is a 'not yet adopted' style divergence that could close if CDC issues an updated regimen guideline -- re-verify before reuse in a future vignette-generation run.

rows.decision_point: Does the TB program provide a direct nutritional cash-transfer benefit to patients during treatment, and if so, how much?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's Ni-kshay Poshan Yojana (NPY) provides a direct benefit transfer to every notified TB patient for the full duration of treatment. Launched at Rs 500/month in April 2018, the benefit was revised upward to Rs 1000/month effective 1 November 2024. From April 2018 to October 2024, Rs 3286.40 crore had been disbursed to over 1.16 crore beneficiaries.

ntep_citation.doc: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, "Initiatives & Achievements-2024" (Press Information Bureau)

rows.western_position: CDC's own annual TB surveillance reporting for the US national program describes case counts, demographics, and treatment outcomes, with no mention of an equivalent direct nutritional cash-transfer benefit paid to TB patients during treatment.

western_citation.doc: CDC, "TB in the US, 2024" -- Executive Commentary

rows.notes: The western_position is a documented absence (CDC's own program reporting does not describe a comparable mechanism), not a positive statement that no such program exists anywhere in the US health system -- flagged as an inference from omission. This corrects the prior draft's 'Rs 500/month' figure, which is now out of date.

rows.decision_point: Beyond the government DBT, is there a structured community-donor program supplementing nutritional support for TB patients?
rows.ntep_position: The Ni-kshay Mitra Initiative (launched September 2022, current guidance dated January 2026) mobilizes registered community 'donors' (individuals, corporates, civil-society groups) to provide supplementary nutritional food-basket support alongside the Nikshay Poshan Yojana DBT. As of January 2026, over 7 lakh Ni-kshay Mitras were registered, supporting 22+ lakh patients with 49+ lakh food baskets distributed.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, Guidance Document on Ni-kshay Mitra Initiative 2026

rows.western_position: CDC's national TB program reporting describes no equivalent structured, government-facilitated community-donor adoption/food-basket program operating alongside clinical TB care.

western_citation.doc: CDC, "TB in the US, 2024" -- Executive Commentary

rows.notes: Same absence-based western citation caveat as DIV-013. Keep this row distinct from DIV-013 in vignettes -- Ni-kshay Mitra is a community-donor layer, not the DBT itself.

rows.decision_point: Is every diagnosed TB case reported into a single centralized, case-based national platform linked to patient benefit payments, or reported through decentralized state/local public health surveillance?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's Nikshay platform is the single case-based system of record used simultaneously for notification, treatment tracking, and DBT (Nikshay Poshan Yojana) disbursement -- linking a patient's notification status directly to their nutritional benefit eligibility.

ntep_citation.doc: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, "Initiatives & Achievements-2024" (PIB)

rows.western_position: US TB cases are reported through the National Tuberculosis Surveillance System (NTSS), run through state/local health department reporting to CDC, with no equivalent single platform linking a specific patient's case notification to a direct cash-benefit disbursement.

western_citation.doc: CDC, "TB in the US, 2024" -- Executive Commentary

rows.decision_point: Is this patient's case more likely to have been identified through a proactive, program-run active case-finding drive in a defined high-risk population, versus through the patient's own care-seeking followed by contact investigation?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP runs systematic active case-finding (ACF) -- house-to-house searches -- targeted at defined high-risk groups (PLHIV, diabetics, undernourished persons, residents of prisons/asylums/old-age-homes/orphanages, tribal areas, marginalized populations), which had diagnosed an additional 3 lakh TB cases over the prior 6 years as of the 2024 report.

ntep_citation.doc: Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, "Initiatives & Achievements-2024" (PIB)

rows.western_position: The 2017 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline's discussion of pediatric case identification frames the primary US case-finding mechanism as contact investigation following a known adult/adolescent index case, consistent with a predominantly passive, contact-investigation-driven case-finding model rather than population-level house-to-house ACF drives.

western_citation.doc: Lewinsohn DM et al., Diagnosis of Tuberculosis in Adults and Children, Clin Infect Dis 2017;64(2):e1-e33
western_citation.section: Discussion of contact investigation as the identification pathway (p. e19 area)

rows.decision_point: Is there a standardized, threshold-based national triage protocol that mandates referral to a higher-level facility when specific vital-sign/lab red flags are met?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's Differentiated TB Care framework specifies explicit, quantified red-flag criteria (e.g., SpO2 <94%, respiratory rate >24/min, systolic BP <90 or >140 mmHg, random blood glucose >=200 mg/dl with symptoms or HbA1c >=6.5%, BMI <14 kg/m2, CD4 <100 cells/uL) that mandate escalation/referral to a higher-tier facility as a mandatory activity.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guidance on Differentiated TB Care (March 2025)
ntep_citation.section: Box 4.3, Differentiated TB Care Evaluation, Triaging & Management (p. 19)

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline discusses baseline evaluation and monitoring for adverse effects and treatment response, but leaves hospitalization/referral decisions to individualized clinical judgment rather than a codified, quantified, nationally standardized threshold-based triage protocol comparable to NTEP's Box 4.3.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195
western_citation.section: Recommended baseline and follow-up evaluations discussion (p. 7)

rows.notes: The western_position here is partly an absence claim (no equivalent standardized protocol identified in the fetched document) rather than a quoted contrary rule -- flagged as lower-confidence than DIV-001/002.

rows.decision_point: Is glucose/HbA1c testing performed on every TB patient as part of a structured comorbidity triage, or only on patients with specific diabetes risk factors?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's Differentiated TB Care triage tool includes specific glycemic thresholds (random blood glucose >=200 mg/dl with symptoms, fasting blood glucose >=126 mg/dl, PPBS >=200 mg/dl, or HbA1c >=6.5%) as red-flag criteria evaluated as part of the mandatory triage activities applied to TB patients broadly, not gated on independent diabetes risk factors.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guidance on Differentiated TB Care (March 2025)

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline recommends fasting glucose or HbA1c testing only for patients with American Diabetes Association risk factors for diabetes (age >45 years, BMI >25 kg/m2, first-degree relative with diabetes, or specified race/ethnicity), not as a testing step applied to every TB patient regardless of risk factors.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195

rows.notes: A vignette with a TB patient who does NOT meet ADA risk-factor criteria (e.g., young, normal BMI, no family history) should still get glucose/HbA1c testing as an expected NTEP-arm action, but it would not be an expected western_control-arm action for that same risk-factor-negative patient.

rows.decision_point: Is cotrimoxazole preventive therapy (CPT) given to all people living with HIV who have active TB, regardless of CD4 count?
rows.ntep_position: NTEP's differentiated-care intake documentation tracks CPT status as a standard field for every HIV-reactive TB patient (alongside ART status), and NTEP's TPT addendum lists a cotrimoxazole-containing fixed-dose formulation as 'a preferred formulation in PLHIV' without conditioning it on a CD4 threshold -- consistent with the WHO position of universal CPT for all HIV-positive TB patients regardless of CD4 count.

ntep_citation.doc: Central TB Division, National Guidance on Differentiated TB Care (March 2025); 1HP TPT addendum (Dec 2024)
ntep_citation.section: Differentiated Care intake form, comorbidity/HIV section (p. 86); 1HP addendum dosage footnote (p. 2)

rows.western_position: The 2016 ATS/CDC/IDSA guideline states explicitly that although WHO recommends cotrimoxazole for all HIV-infected people with active TB regardless of CD4 count, 'in high-income countries, co-trimoxazole is primarily used in HIV-infected patients with CD4 counts <200 cells/uL' -- a materially narrower, CD4-gated indication.

western_citation.doc: Nahid P et al., Treatment of Drug-Susceptible Tuberculosis, Clin Infect Dis 2016;63(7):e147-e195

rows.notes: This divergence is stated explicitly in the western_citation source itself (a direct WHO-vs-high-income-country contrast), making it one of the better-grounded rows in this table despite the NTEP side being assembled from two documents' incidental mentions rather than one dedicated CPT policy statement.
